We represent more than 100 child welfare programs across the state, all of the foster care agencies in New York City. I present a few budget priorities. One is workforce. New York City contracted agencies continue to face significant challenges on staff turnover, lack of pay parity for an undercompensated workforce. Nonprofits cannot operate programs without adequate staffing. We ask the Council to continue funding at 3 percent COLA in the FY27 budget. We ask the Council to pass wage equity legislation, Intro. 452 of 2026, which would align nonprofit government human service job titles and raise salaries for nonprofit workers. Hi, good afternoon Chair Stevens and Members of the Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to testify. My name is Sierra Kraft and I’m the Executive Director of the I CARE Coalition. A network of legal service providers dedicated to offering free legal representation to immigrant children and youth facing deportation in New York City. Every year, roughly 5,000 unaccompanied immigrant children arrive in New York and are forced to navigate one of the most complex legal systems in our country, often without a lawyer. Last year, the

Council made a critical investment in legal services for immigrant youth and that investment has already been life changing. It has allowed providers to expand capacity, reduce our shared waitlists and reach more young people who would otherwise have been forced to face court during one of the most vulnerable moments of their lives. The conditions are rapidly worsening and they’re being treated as enforcement priorities by this administration. Children's cases are getting fast tracked, even when they don’t have an attorney. They’re being asked to defend themselves in proceedings so complex that even trained lawyers struggle to navigate them and at the same time, we’re seeing youth apprehended within our communities and sponsors and guardians are increasingly afraid to come forward for fear of detention or deportation themselves. We recently encountered a 14 year old girl who was picked up in Texas and transported away from her family to a shelter in Brooklyn. She had already appeared in immigration court five times without a lawyer. At her third hearing, the judge took pleadings directly from her and told her if she did

not apply for legal relief, she would be deported. No child should ever be placed in that position and when children have a lawyer, they’re chances of securing protection rise to nearly 90 percent. So, today, I CARE respectfully requests the Council to sustain and expand two critical initiatives. The Unaccompanied Minors and Families initiative, which supports eight organizations serving more than 2,000 children and families with direct representation and coordinated services and the special immigrant juvenile status initiatives, which was new last year but helps youth who have experienced parental -
Thank you for your testimony. Time has expired.
And abandonment. Thank you so much.

Starting time.

Good afternoon Chair and members of the Committee. My name is Pete Basica. I am the Founder and Chairman of 360 Smarter Care. Our

current mental health system is built on providing services to our youth when they begin to show signs that they are troubled. It is too little, too late for too many. CDC data shows that 40 percent of the students report persistent depression, sadness or hopelessness and 20 percent have exhibited suicidal ideation. Children in foster care are at even greater risk for attachment disorder and PTSD. This is common knowledge for professionals in this space and I’m sure to members of this Committee. The shortages of qualified professionals to help our youth create long wait times. Unfortunately the need for these services is growing faster than we produced more qualified mental health professionals. The solution is prevention through behavioral education. Assigning more work to teachers who are already overwhelmed is not a solution. New York must invest in preventative behavioral, emotional and mental health education delivered through scalable digital tools that reach our youth early, consistently, across every school and community.

The 360 Smarter Self program is a digital prevention platform that helps young people develop the resilience and mental strength necessary to navigate our complex society. Smarter Self can support New York's youth, evenings, weekends, and the 180 days a year they are not in school. As you consider the fiscal year 2027 budget, I urge you to consider the need to immediately begin with education and prevention in addition to the efforts that come unfortunately all too often too little, too late. Thank you for your time.
Thank you for your testimony. Kevin McEwen, you may begin when the Sergeant starts your clock.
Starting time.

Good afternoon Chair and Members of the Committee on Children and Youth. My name is Kevin McEwen and I am the Executive Director of the Kofago Institute. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. Support of our 2027 funding requests and the children and youth that we serve in New York City.

Kofago Institute uses arts and culture as tools for youth development education, identity building and opportunity. Our work is especially important to young people in communities that are under-resourced and too often overlooked. One of our most important initiatives called Kofago Taraji is our Summer Youth Employment program and through the program, young people receive paid opportunities to build workforce skills, leadership, confidence and cultural knowledge through the arts. Kofago Taraji is more than a summer job, it is an investment into the future of our youth. We also support K-12 programming across New York City and host the Kofago conference and the Cultural Rise, a dance conference which creates meaningful opportunities for youth, families, educators, and communities to engage in learning mentorship, performance and cultural exchange. We have submitted requests for support because the need is urgent and the demand continues to grow. Our children and youth deserve programs that affirm who they are and expand what they believe is possible.

We respectfully ask the Committee to support the Kofago Institutes 2027 request. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Hi, my name is Allison Hollihan and I am the Director of the New York Initiative for children of incarcerated parents at the Osborne Association. I want to give a big shout out to all of the young people who just testified today. I am here to talk about the needs of the one of 14 children who have experienced parental incarceration. First, New York City must safeguard children when a parent is arrested. We are grateful to receive Council funding in the past to implement the 2019 Safeguarding Children of a Parent, Parents Law and we’ve trained 9,000 of the 34,000 uniformed officers and requested funding from the Council to continue this work and to also train DOC personnel to minimize stress for children visiting Rikers and safeguarding

them when their caregiver is arrested when they are visiting their parent. We urge the Council to introduce a bill requiring NYPD to collect data on the number of children present during an arrest to ensure targeted community resources are available for these children and to safeguard children when planning for and executing warrants. The city must prevent the criminalization of children speaking with their incarcerated parents. DOC contracts with Secures who collects data during phone calls and sells it to law enforcement customers nationwide. Passing the ECHOES Act Intro. 96 will protect children from being surveilled and criminalized for simply talking on the phone with their parent who is incarcerated on Rikers. We urge city agencies, especially ACS, to collect data on how many children experience the arrest or incarceration of a parent to inform service delivery, resources allocation and cross systems collaboration. We ask for children of incarcerated parents to be considered as a priority population for Summer Youth Employment program for the one in five high school students experiencing parental incarceration. The

Interagency Coordinating Council on Youth should create a working group focused on youth with incarcerated parents to improve the effectiveness of youth serving agencies to meet their unique needs. Finally, it is critical for the Council to monitor the implementation of Local Law 40 passed last year requiring DOC to have child friendly visiting spaces, reduce visit wait times for children and train DOC personnel on how to minimize stress for child visitors.

Good afternoon. My name is Nicole Carta with Healing New York. Thank you Chair Stevens and the Committee for the opportunity to testify today. Founded in 1875, is the New York Society for the prevention of cruelty to children. Healing New York is the nation's first child protection agency.

Today, our work focuses on two core areas, clinical services and prevention. Our clinical services include trauma recovery for children who have experienced child abuse and neglect. Using evidence based therapy, our bilingual clinicians helped children address anxiety, depression, fear and post traumatic stress disorder. We are a referral partner of ACS, the city’s foster care agencies and other child serving organizations. Children could receive in person and virtual therapeutic care at no cost for as long as they need to recover. We also provide therapeutic supervised visitation for families referred by the court system. These visits include coaching and therapy groups for both visiting and custodial parents to help families heal. We are one of only two providers of therapeutic supervised visitation in the city and the only one that offers it free of charge to families. This year, we opened our family healing center with an emergency cash assistance program for urgent needs like utility bills and groceries. We’re also working with a coalition of partners to help connect our families to broader social services when needed. Our

approach ensures we are addressing the whole picture of need to help families stabilize. Last year, we served clients in 39 Council Districts, almost all of whom are low income and come predominantly from Black and Latinx communities. Our second program, the trailing - the Training Institute focuses on prevention. We educate children, caregivers and professionals about sexual abuse and online sexual exportation. Our school based programs fulfill the annual requirement under New York State's Aaron’s Law. We also train parents and caregivers on how to talk with children on these difficult topics and support professionals in identifying, reporting and preventing abuse and recognizing and managing their own secondary trauma. Last year, we had school trainings in 21 Council districts. We currently have a waitlist for our programs, Council funding would allow Healing New York to hire additional therapists -

Good afternoon. Thank you Chair Stevens and the Committee on Children and Youth for the opportunity to testify today. My name is

Benjamin Tocker and I am here on behalf of my colleagues at Graham Wyndham. Graham has been providing support and services to children and families for 220 years and we’re deeply committed to supporting our families and the needs of their school aged children. So, I’m here today to talk about how important it is for students to have reliable school transportation starting as soon as they’re placed in foster care or as soon as they switch placements. For students in care, being able to stay at their home school can be one of the only sources of stability during a very difficult and traumatic time for them. State and Federal law recognizes the importance of this stability and they require New York City Public School Districts to provide transportation. However, this transportation can often take weeks or months to be arranged. There are a few examples demonstrating why the city must provide interim transportation for these students who are in foster care and awaiting bus services. We have foster parents who are facing repercussions at work because they are escorting students to and from school.

There are agency staff who are kept from doing other more important work because they’re spending up to four hours or more every day securing the transportation for these students. And students, although they have rideshare provided for them, they are only able to use it when there is a chaperone and so, if they do not have a chaperone, they’re unable to access the rideshare. So, some of the solutions that we’re advocating for are that the city could contract the transportation providers who are already using vetted drivers and who do not require chaperones such as Kid Car, which is operating in New York City currently. Using ACS or other city owned vehicles that include escorts, which is done for students at the Children Center. Creating dedicated interim transportation services for these students. Hiring chaperone aids to accompany the students or at the very least, reimbursing the parents or the staff or the chaperones who are currently setting up to fill the gap and we respectfully ask that the city does more to support these students in foster care by investing $3 million to provide interim transportation services.
